<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but B's rebuttals did more damage to A's core architecture. B repeatedly forced A into defending a conditional, unbuilt "ideal" privacy-preserving credential system rather than the mandates governments actually implement, and A's own admission ("I am not claiming national deployment") let B frame A's whole case as aspirational. B's sharpest hit was showing that A's central "coverage gap" argument (provider checks protect kids whose caregivers never enable household controls) is self-undermining: the same negligent-household children most likely to lack parental oversight are also the ones most likely to route around a website-level gate via VPNs, siblings' devices, or offshore sites — meaning the mandate doesn't close the gap, it relocates the risk to less-safe corners. A's answer in closing ("not therefore a child who will defeat every provider-side check") was a bare assertion rather than a developed rebuttal, leaving this key structural point only partially answered. B also raised an unanswered burden-of-proof point (PRO proposes the change, so PRO bears the burden on displacement harm) that A never squarely engaged. A's case on privacy-preserving design and proportionality was solid and internally consistent, and its distinction between disqualifying implementations and the underlying duty was a fair reading of the motion, but it never fully neutralized B's practical and structural pressure. On balance, B made the debate easier to decide by landing the more decisive, harder-to-answer rebuttals.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's rebuttal 2 point that negligent-caregiver households are simultaneously the households most likely to evade website-level age checks (VPN/sibling device/offshore site), which undercuts A's central "coverage gap" justification for the mandate and was never fully rebutted beyond assertion in A's closing.</best_rebuttal>
